## Transformations

::: {.callout title="Definition 12.1"}
Let $X$ be a random variable with CDF $F_X(x)$. A **transformation** of $X$ is any function $Y = g(X)$ and the CDF of the transformed random variable $Y$ is $F_Y(y)$. If $X$ is discrete, then $Y$ is also discrete with PMF $P_Y(y)$. If $X$ is continuous and $g$ is a continuous function, then $Y$ is continuous with PDF $f_Y(y)$.
:::

## Ex: Uniform Probabilities

::: {.callout title="Example 12.1"}
Let $X$ be a discrete random variable with PMF $P_X(x) = \frac{1}{10} \text{ for } x \in \{1, 2, 3, \dots, 10\}$. Let $Y = g(X) = 2X$.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- 100000
pmf_x <- rep(1/10, 10)
X <- sample(1:10, n, replace = TRUE, prob = pmf_x)
Y <- 2*X
```

```{r}
pmf_Y <- table(Y)/length(Y)
x0 <- seq(2, 18, 2)
x1 <- seq(4, 20, 2)
cdf_Y <- cumsum(pmf_Y)
y0 <- cdf_Y[1:9]
y1 <- cdf_Y[1:9]

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(pmf_Y, ylab = "Probability", main = "PMF of Y")
points(names(pmf_Y), pmf_Y, pch = 19)

plot(names(pmf_Y), cdf_Y, pch = 19, 
     main = "CDF of Y", ylab = "Probability", xlab = "Y")
points(x1, y1)
segments(x0, y0, x1, y1)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
:::

## Ex: Five Coin Flips

::: {.callout title="Example 12.2"}
Let $X$ be a discrete random variable with PMF $P_X(x) = \frac{\binom{5}{x}}{2^5} \text{ for } x \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$. Let $Y = g(X) = X^2$.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- 100000
pmf_x <- choose(5, 0:5)/2^5
X <- sample(0:5, n, replace = TRUE, prob = pmf_x)
Y <- X^2
```

```{r}
pmf_Y <- table(Y)/length(Y)
x0 <- c(0, 1, 4, 9, 16)
x1 <- c(1, 4, 9, 16, 25)
cdf_Y <- cumsum(pmf_Y)
y0 <- cdf_Y[1:5]
y1 <- cdf_Y[1:5]

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(pmf_Y, ylab = "Probability", main = "PMF of Y")
points(names(pmf_Y), pmf_Y, pch = 19)

plot(names(pmf_Y), cdf_Y, pch = 19, 
     main = "CDF of Y", ylab = "Probability", xlab = "Y")
points(x1, y1)
segments(x0, y0, x1, y1)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
:::

## Ex: Constant Density

::: {.callout title="Example 12.3"}
Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with PDF $f_X(x) = 1 \text{ for } x \in (0, 1)$. Let $Y = g(X) = -\ln(X)$.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- 100000
X <- runif(n, 0, 1)
Y <- -log(X)
```

```{r}
y_seq <- seq(0, 12, length = 1000)
cdf_Y <- sapply(y_seq, function(y) mean(Y <= y))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(Y, freq = FALSE)

plot(y_seq, cdf_Y, type = 'l', main = "CDF of Y",
     ylab = "Probability", xlab = "Y")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
:::

## Ex: Density on (0, 1)

::: {.callout title="Example 12.4"}
Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with PDF $f_X(x) = 6x(1-x) \text{ for } x \in (0, 1)$. Let $Y = g(X) = X^2$.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- 100000
X <- rbeta(n, 2, 2)
Y <- X^2
```

```{r}
y_seq <- seq(0, 1, length = 1000)
cdf_Y <- sapply(y_seq, function(y) mean(Y <= y))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(Y, freq = FALSE)

plot(y_seq, cdf_Y, type = 'l', main = "CDF of Y",
     ylab = "Probability", xlab = "Y")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
:::

## PMF of Discrete Transformations

::: {.callout title="Theorem 12.1"}
Let $X$ be a discrete random variable with PMF $P_X(x)$. Let $g(X)$ be a strictly monotonic transformation on the support for $X$, $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$. Then the PMF for $Y$ is:

$$
P_Y(y) = 
\begin{cases}
P_X(g^{-1}(y)) &\text{if } y \in \{g(x)|x \in \mathcal{X}\} \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$
:::

## PMF of Discrete Transformations (Proof)

Let $Y=g(X)$ where $X$ is a discrete random variable. If $g$ is strictly monotonic on $\mathcal{X}$, then it is a one-to-one and invertible function, so $g^{-1}$ exists and every $x \in \mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ maps to exactly one $y \in \mathcal{Y}$. Then, for any $y \in \{g(x) | x \in \mathcal{X}\}$

$$
\begin{align}
P_Y(y) &= P(Y = y) \\
&= P(g(X) = y) \\
&= P(X = g^{-1}(y)) \\
&= P_X(g^{-1}(y))
\end{align}
$$

and is $0$ otherwise.

## Ex: Uniform Probabilities

::: {.callout title="Example 12.5"}
Let $X$ be a discrete random variable with PMF:

$$
P_X(x) = 
\begin{cases}
\frac{1}{10} &\text{for } x \in \{1, 2, \dots, 10\} \\
0 &\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

Find the PMF for $Y$ where $Y = g(X) = X^2$
:::

. . .

The function $g(x)$ is strictly increasing with inverse $g^{-1}(y) = \sqrt{y}$ for $y = g(x) \in \{1, 4, 9, \dots, 100\}$. Since $P_Y(y) = P_X(g^{-1}(y)) = \frac{1}{10}$, then:

$$
P_Y(y) = 
\begin{cases}
\frac{1}{10} &\text{if } y \in \{1, 4, 9, \dots, 100\} \\
0 &\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

## CDF of Discrete Transformations

::: {.callout title="Theorem 12.2"}
Let $X$ be a discrete random variable with CDF $F_X(x)$. Let $g(X)$ be a strictly monotonic transformation on the support for $X$, $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$. Then the CDF for $Y$ is:

$$
F_Y(y) = 
\begin{cases}
F_X(g^{-1}(y)) &\text{if } g \text{ is increasing} \\
1-F_X(g^{-1}(y)-1) &\text{if } g \text{ is decreasing}
\end{cases}
$$
:::

## CDF of Discrete Transformations (Proof)

Let $Y=g(X)$ where $X$ is a discrete random variable. If $g$ is strictly monotonic on $\mathcal{X}$, then it is a one-to-one and invertible function, so $g^{-1}$ exists and every $x \in \mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ maps to exactly one $y \in \mathcal{Y}$. Then, for any $y$:

$$
\begin{align}
F_Y(y) &= P(Y \leq y) \\
&= P(g(X) \leq y) \text{ if } \\
&= 
\begin{cases}
P(X \leq g^{-1}(y)) &\text{ if } g \text{ is increasing} \\
P(X \geq g^{-1}(y)) &\text{ if } g \text{ is decreasing}
\end{cases} \\
&=
\begin{cases}
P(X \leq g^{-1}(y)) &\text{ if } g \text{ is increasing} \\
1 - P(X \leq g^{-1}(y)-1) &\text{ if } g \text{ is decreasing}
\end{cases} \\
&=
\begin{cases}
F_X(g^{-1}(y)) &\text{if } g \text{ is increasing} \\
1-F_X(g^{-1}(y)-1) &\text{if } g \text{ is decreasing}
\end{cases} \\
\end{align}
$$

## Ex: Dice Roll

::: {.callout title="Example 12.8"}
Let $X$ be a discrete random variable with CDF:

$$
F_X(x) =
\begin{cases}
0 &\text{for } x < 1 \\
\frac{\lfloor x \rfloor}{6} &\text {for } 1 \leq x \leq 6 \\
1 &\text{for } x > 6
\end{cases}
$$

Find the CDF of $Y$ where $Y = g(X) = 7 - X$.
:::

. . .

The function $g(x) = 7 - x$ is strictly decreasing with inverse $g^{-1}(y) = 7-y$ where $y = g(x) \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$. Since $1-F_X(g^{-1}(y)-1) = 1-F_X(7 - y  - 1) = 1-\frac{\lfloor 6-y \rfloor}{6} = \frac{\lfloor y \rfloor}{6}$, then:

$$
F_Y(y) = 
\begin{cases}
0 &\text{for } y < 1 \\
\frac{\lfloor y \rfloor}{6} &\text{for } 1 \leq y \leq 6 \\
1 &\text{for } y > 6
\end{cases}
$$

## CDF of Continuous Transformations

::: {.callout title="Theorem 12.3"}
Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with CDF $F_X(x)$. Let $g(X)$ be a strictly monotonic transformation on the support for $X$, $\mathcal{X}$. Then the CDF for $Y$ is:

$$
F_Y(y) = 
\begin{cases}
F_X(g^{-1}(y)) &\text{if } g \text{ is increasing} \\
1-F_X(g^{-1}(y)) &\text{if } g \text{ is decreasing}
\end{cases}
$$
:::

## CDF of Continuous Transformations (Proof)

Let $Y=g(X)$ where $X$ is a continuous random variable. If $g$ is strictly monotonic on $\mathcal{X}$, then it is a one-to-one and invertible function, so $g^{-1}$ exists and every $x \in \mathcal{X}$ maps to exactly one $y \in \mathcal{Y}$. Then, for any $y$:

$$
\begin{align}
F_Y(y) &= P(Y \leq y) \\
&= P(g(X) \leq y) \text{ if } \\
&= 
\begin{cases}
P(X \leq g^{-1}(y)) &\text{ if } g \text{ is increasing} \\
P(X \geq g^{-1}(y)) &\text{ if } g \text{ is decreasing}
\end{cases} \\
&=
\begin{cases}
P(X \leq g^{-1}(y)) &\text{ if } g \text{ is increasing} \\
1 - P(X \leq g^{-1}(y)) &\text{ if } g \text{ is decreasing}
\end{cases} \\
&=
\begin{cases}
F_X(g^{-1}(y)) &\text{if } g \text{ is increasing} \\
1-F_X(g^{-1}(y)) &\text{if } g \text{ is decreasing}
\end{cases} \\
\end{align}
$$

and is $0$ otherwise.

## Ex: Constant Density (1)

::: {.callout title="Example 12.11"}
Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with CDF:

$$
F_X(x) =
\begin{cases}
0 &\text{for } x \leq 0 \\
x &\text{for } 0 < x < 1 \\
1 &\text{for } x \geq 1
\end{cases}
$$

Find the CDF of $Y$ where $Y = g(X) = -\ln(X)$.
:::

. . .

The function $g(x) = -\ln(x)$ is strictly decreasing. The inverse is $g^{-1}(y) = e^{-y}$ where $y = g(x) \in (0, \infty)$. Since $F_Y(y) = 1-F_X(g^{-1}(y)) = 1-e^{-y}$, then

$$
F_Y(y) =
\begin{cases}
0 &\text{for } y \leq 0 \\
1-e^{-y} &\text{for } 0 < y < \infty \\
\end{cases}
$$

## PDF of Continuous Transformations

::: {.callout title="Theorem 12.4"}
Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with PDF $f_X(x)$. Let $g(X)$ be a strictly monotonic transformation on the support for $X$, $\mathcal{X}$. Then the PDF for $Y$ is:

$$
f_Y(y) = 
\begin{cases}
f_X(g^{-1}(y)) \left\lvert \frac{d}{dy} g^{-1}(y) \right\rvert &\forall y \ni y = g(x)\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$
:::

## PDF of Continuous Transformations (Proof)

Let $Y=g(X)$ where $X$ is a continuous random variable. If $g$ is strictly monotonic on $\mathcal{X}$, then it is a one-to-one and invertible function, so $g^{-1}$ exists and every $x \in \mathcal{X}$ maps to exactly one $y \in \mathcal{Y}$. Then, for any $y$ where $y = g(x)$:

$$
\begin{align}
f_Y(y) &= \frac{d}{dy} F_Y(y) \\
&=
\begin{cases}
\frac{d}{dy} F_X(g^{-1}(y)) &\text{if } g \text{ is increasing} \\
\frac{d}{dy} \left[1-F_X(g^{-1}(y))\right] &\text{if } g \text{ is decreasing}
\end{cases} \\
&=
\begin{cases}
f_X(g^{-1}(y)) \frac{d}{dy} g^{-1}(y) &\text{if } g \text{ is increasing} \\
-f_X(g^{-1}(y)) \frac{d}{dy} g^{-1}(y) &\text{if } g \text{ is decreasing}
\end{cases} \\
&= f_X(g^{-1}(y)) \left\lvert \frac{d}{dy} g^{-1}(y) \right\rvert
\end{align}
$$

## Ex: Density on (0, 5)

::: {.callout title="Example 12.14"}
Let $X$ be a random variable with PDF:

$$
f_X(x) = 
\begin{cases}
\frac{2}{25} (5 - x) &\text{for } x \in (0, 5) \\
0 &\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

Find the PDF of $Y$ where $Y = g(X) = X^2$
:::

. . .

The function $g(x) = x^2$ is strictly increasing on $(0, 5)$. The inverse is $g^{-1}(y) = \sqrt{y}$ where $y \in (0, 25)$. Since $f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y))\left| \frac{d}{dy} g^{-1}(y)\right| = \frac{2}{25}(5 - \sqrt{y}) \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}$, then:

$$
f_Y(y) = 
\begin{cases}
\frac{5 - \sqrt{y}}{25\sqrt{y}} &\text{for } y \in (0, 25) \\
0 &\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$
